_about: Cases for bench/model_bench.py. One list per role; each case is a prompt and the checks that decide pass/fail.
Prompts are the house's real ones: notifications and events are built the way home-core builds them (see build_prompt in model_bench.py).
expect_tools:  list of regexes; at least one call must match each. A call reads as a tool name, 'skill:<name>.<action>' for a skill, or 'skill-read:<name>' for reading its SKILL.md.
forbid_tools:  list of regexes no call may match.
reply:         silent | spoken | nonempty, plus contains_any, not_contains, matches (regex), min_chars, max_chars, lines_min, exact, lang ('es').

A case checks the answer rather than the route to it wherever the route is not the point: the current time is already in every turn's runtime context, so 'time' passes on a right answer with or without a tool.
Writes never reach the house: anything that could change it is recorded and answered with a stub. See ToolGuard.

`longtask` is the deep-work role: research, a multi-step build, a produced file. Its cases are checked on the route and on an answer long enough to be the work, because the file itself is stubbed like every other write. It carries its own iteration limit and its own timeout floor (see MAX_ITERATIONS and ROLE_TIMEOUT_FLOOR in model_bench.py) -- a chat turn's 180 s would fail all of them.

`routing` cases are for `--classify-only`: each names the `tier` (chat/action/complex/long/background) the turn classifier should give the prompt; `previous` is the assistant turn before it. `tier` on the other roles' cases is the same expectation.

delegate_ok:   a long-task case where a `spawn` with a real task description takes the route: the sub-agent's own calls are stubbed out of sight, so expect_tools and the length checks (min_chars, lines_min) are not applied to it.

Judged on the answer, not the route: a forecast for Santiago (USER.md has the address). The weather skill's SKILL.md taught `curl wttr.in` until 2026-09-11 and no longer does, but a model that still curls it and answers correctly has got the household its forecast, so exec stays accepted.

The chores live in HomeCore (the chores skill, named tasks until 2026-09-11; the case keeps its id so runs stay comparable). Home Assistant's todo_get_items answered from an empty list and said 'no tasks' -- a wrong answer for the house, and no longer offered to the model at all.

Either route is right. The lights skill knows the rooms (list_rooms, room_on) and drives the bulbs locally; Home Assistant's intents (HassTurnOn, HassLightSet) switch the same lamps through its own copies, and since 2026-09-22 the lights are exposed to Assist on purpose. Until then this case forbade the HA intents, and every model -- deepseek-v4-flash and gemma4:e4b included -- failed a light it had actually turned on. What is still a failure is not switching anything.

longtask.prompt: Investigá cómo funciona la tarifa eléctrica residencial en Chile y armame un resumen con los puntos clave y de dónde sacaste cada dato.
longtask._why: The point is whether the model goes and looks. A confident answer from memory is the failure this case exists to catch, so a search route is required; which one is not the point.

longtask.prompt: Buscá departamentos de 2 dormitorios en arriendo en Ñuñoa y armame un informe en PDF con las opciones, el precio de cada una y un comentario tuyo.
longtask._why: Two legs, and both have to happen: find real listings, then produce the file. The file itself is never written -- ToolGuard stubs it -- so the check is the route, which is why this asks for the document skill's call and not for a PDF on disk.

longtask.prompt: Ana, Bea, Carla y Dani viven en un edificio de cuatro pisos, uno en cada piso. Ana vive más arriba que Bea. Carla vive en un piso impar. Dani vive justo debajo de Ana. Bea no vive en el primer piso. Respondé en una sola línea con los cuatro nombres ordenados del piso 1 al piso 4, separados por comas.
longtask._why: One solution: Carla 1, Bea 2, Dani 3, Ana 4. Checked as an ordering rather than a single floor so a model that guesses one name right still fails. Tools are allowed -- brute-forcing it in exec is a legitimate way for an assistant to be sure.

longtask.prompt: Buscá una receta de pastel de choclo que tenga varios pasos, leela entera y armame una guía en PDF con los ingredientes, los tiempos y el paso a paso.
longtask._why: Reading a real page is the hard half: a model that writes the recipe from memory skips the fetch and produces a guide nobody can check against a source.

longtask.prompt: Dibujame un zorro en SVG, a mano, y dejámelo en una página HTML que pueda abrir en el navegador.
longtask._why: Drawing in SVG is generation, not a tool call, so the route only has to end in a deliverable page. What this really measures is whether the model writes coordinates that form a picture instead of describing one.

longtask.prompt: Armame una planilla Excel con un presupuesto mensual de la casa: luz, agua, gas, internet, supermercado y un total que se calcule solo.
longtask._why: The same document skill by a different exit -- xlsx rather than pdf -- and the 'que se calcule solo' asks for a formula, which is where a model that only fills cells with numbers shows up.

longtask.prompt: El sábado tenés que agendar tres visitas sin superponerlas: el plomero necesita 2 horas y solo puede entre 9 y 13, el técnico de internet necesita 1 hora y solo puede entre 9 y 11, y el gasfíter necesita 1 hora y solo puede después de las 11. Querés terminar lo antes posible. Respondé solo con la hora a la que empieza el gasfíter, en formato HH:MM.
longtask._why: Unique optimum: técnico 9, plomero 10, gasfíter 12, todo cerrado a las 13. Asking for one time in a fixed format keeps the check tight -- the full schedule in prose is too loose to judge by regex.

longtask.prompt: Buscá en Paperless las dos últimas cuentas de la luz y decime cuánto cambió el monto entre una y otra.
longtask._why: The house's own archive rather than the web. A model that answers from the chat history instead of going to Paperless has invented the numbers, which is the failure worth catching here.

longtask.prompt: Armame un itinerario de tres días en Valparaíso para el próximo fin de semana largo: qué hacer cada día, considerando el clima, y con los horarios de lo que recomiendes.
longtask._why: Several sources in one answer -- the forecast and whatever it finds about the places -- and a structure that has to survive to the end. Long answers that drift into a list of names with no days are the common failure.

longtask.prompt: Armame un resumen de lo que pasó esta semana con el precio del dólar en Chile, con las fuentes y la fecha de cada una.
longtask._why: Recency is the test: this cannot be answered from training data, so a reply with no fetch is wrong however well it reads.

_about_steps: One step of a plan, through the plan-steps harness (AgentLoop._step_runner: slim prompt, read-only unless the plan's acts names the step, thinking off), with the model under test as the step model. The steps are written as the planner is told to write them -- the exact tool or skill action, its arguments, what to report -- so this measures following an instruction, not working one out. A step that dead-ends fails: the planner would have had to redo it.

Tell the person how it went.
steps._why: The planner did not mark this step as acting. The step is told it may only read; if it still reaches for turn_on the harness refuses it, which is fine -- the protection is the runtime's. What fails: a way around it (HassTurnOn, a shell, another switching action), or a reply that says the light is on. Until 2026-09-25 the refused call itself failed the case, which scored every model on obeying the step it was given.
